column1: What is the key functional difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation?
column2: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel by class without distinguishing individual object instances, whereas instance segmentation identifies and separately masks each distinct object instance.

column1: In computer vision segmentation tasks, how do "things" differ from "stuff"?
column2: "Things" are countable objects with distinct shapes and instance identities (e.g., cats, cars), while "stuff" consists of amorphous, uncountable background regions (e.g., sky, grass, water).

column1: Why are fully convolutional networks for semantic segmentation typically designed with downsampling followed by upsampling, rather than operating entirely at full image resolution?
column2: Operating at full resolution throughout all deep layers is computationally and memory prohibitive, whereas downsampling compresses spatial size to build deeper semantic context before upsampling recovers spatial detail.

column1: How does max-unpooling utilize saved information from previous max-pooling layers to restore spatial resolution?
column2: Max-unpooling records the exact spatial indices of maximum values during max-pooling and places upsampled features back into those specific stored index locations while filling remaining entries with zeros.

column1: What spatial operation defines a transpose convolution (also called a fractionally strided convolution)?
column2: It takes a low-resolution input pixel, multiplies it by a learned filter kernel, and pastes the scaled output onto an overlapping region in a higher-resolution output map.

column1: Mathematically, why is transpose convolution named "transpose"?
column2: Its forward pass operation corresponds to multiplying the input vector by the transpose matrix ($X^T$) of a standard strided convolution matrix ($X$).

column1: What is the primary function of a $1 \times 1$ convolution in a deep network architecture?
column2: It performs a pixel-wise linear combination across channels to adjust (increase or decrease) channel depth without altering spatial dimensions ($H \times W$).

column1: What is the formula for Intersection over Union (IoU) used to evaluate bounding box or segmentation mask accuracy?
column2: $\text{IoU} = \frac{\text{Area of Overlap}}{\text{Area of Union}} = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$

column1: Why is Intersection over Union (IoU) preferred over raw pixel accuracy when evaluating semantic segmentation models?
column2: Raw pixel accuracy is heavily biased by dominant background classes ("stuff"), whereas IoU measures true overlap per class, accounting for spatial misalignments and class imbalance.

column1: What are the two primary components of the multitask loss function used in standard object detection networks?
column2: A classification loss (e.g., cross-entropy for predicted class) and a localization loss (e.g., $L_1$ or smooth $L_1$ regression for bounding box coordinates).

column1: Why does the Selective Search algorithm prioritize high recall over high precision when generating region proposals?
column2: Subsequent neural network classification stages can easily filter out false positive proposals, but any true object missed during proposal generation (false negative) cannot be recovered.

column1: What was the major computational bottleneck of the original R-CNN architecture?
column2: It cropped and independently ran a full forward pass through a deep CNN for each of the ~2,000 region proposals per image, leading to massive redundant computation.

column1: How did Fast R-CNN overcome the redundant computation bottleneck of R-CNN?
column2: It processes the entire image through the convolutional backbone once to produce a feature map, then crops region proposals directly from that shared feature map.

column1: How does ROI Align differ from standard ROI Pooling in Fast/Faster R-CNN?
column2: ROI Pooling quantizes floating-point ROI boundaries to discrete grid coordinates (causing spatial misalignment), whereas ROI Align uses bilinear interpolation at continuous sampling points without quantization.

column1: What module replaced CPU-based Selective Search in Faster R-CNN to achieve end-to-end proposal generation?
column2: The Region Proposal Network (RPN), a fully convolutional network operating directly on shared feature maps.

column1: In a Region Proposal Network (RPN), what is an anchor box?
column2: A fixed reference bounding box of a specified scale and aspect ratio centered at a spatial position on a feature map, used as a baseline for objectness scoring and coordinate offsets.

column1: What does "end-to-end learning" mean in the context of deep learning object detectors?
column2: The system learns mapping directly from raw image pixels to final detections and bounding boxes via backpropagation, eliminating hand-engineered features or external proposal algorithms.

column1: What is the purpose of Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) during object detection inference?
column2: To eliminate redundant, highly overlapping predicted bounding boxes for the same object by retaining only the box with the highest confidence score and discarding neighboring boxes exceeding an IoU threshold.

column1: Why are bounding box regression targets parameterized as relative offsets ($\Delta x, \Delta y$) and log-scale ratios ($\Delta w, \Delta h$) rather than absolute pixel coordinates?
column2: Relative parameterization makes regression targets scale- and location-invariant, keeping target values normalized near zero for stable neural network training.

column1: What is the primary training advantage of two-stage object detectors (e.g., Faster R-CNN) over naive single-stage detectors?
column2: Stage 1 (RPN) filters out the vast majority of background regions, mitigating the extreme class imbalance between foreground objects and background negatives during Stage 2 classification.

column1: How does the YOLO (You Only Look Once) architecture organize object prediction across an image?
column2: It divides the image into an $S \times S$ grid where each grid cell directly predicts $B$ bounding box offsets, confidence scores, and class probabilities in a single forward pass.

column1: How does the DETR (DEtection TRansformer) architecture eliminate the need for hand-crafted components like anchor boxes and Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)?
column2: It models object detection as a direct set prediction problem using object queries and bipartite matching, producing a fixed set of unique box/class predictions without duplicates.

column1: What algorithm does DETR use during training to uniquely match predicted bounding boxes with ground-truth objects?
column2: The Hungarian matching algorithm, which finds an optimal one-to-one assignment based on a joint class and box loss cost matrix.

column1: What parallel branch does Mask R-CNN add to the Faster R-CNN framework?
column2: A fully convolutional branch that predicts a small binary segmentation mask ($28 \times 28$) per ROI for each candidate object class.

column1: How can Mask R-CNN be adapted to perform human pose estimation?
column2: By framing pose estimation as keypoint detection, where the mask head predicts a set of binary spatial heatmaps/masks corresponding to individual human body joints.

column1: What parameters typically define a 3D bounding box for object detection in 3D space?
column2: 3D center coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$, 3D physical dimensions (width $W$, height $H$, length $L$), and orientation angle (yaw).

column1: In 3D computer vision, how does a point cloud differ from a 3D mesh representation?
column2: A point cloud is an unordered set of isolated 3D surface points, whereas a 3D mesh connects surface vertices with polygonal faces (typically triangles) and surface normals.
